title: The Graces dwell on the addressee's tongue; Dionysus enters the argument
english: You truly carry the Graces themselves upon your tongue, and it seems to me that a precinct of theirs—a temple—has been established for you somewhere here, and it charms the same goddesses: your soul, like a pure plectrum, makes the tongue sound in varied response. That is why they rejoice in it more than when they look upon Naxos, which tradition holds to be the island of the Graces—the place where Dionysus was defeated by Ariadne and lived with her as her husband. But how fittingly Dionysus, the son of Semele, has come into our discussion! If he were not a god, how much accusation he would have received from us, for overlooking a poor man who dreams of taxes even from his very bedding, but is otherwise devoted to the Muses and the Graces.
